An attacker uses the extracted key to make API requests on behalf of the application, bypassing user authentication and rate limiting. Describe API key exposure vectors, detection methods, and secure key management practices.
reasoning_focus: API key hardcoding, client-side secret storage, key extraction from binaries and repositories
expected_answer: API keys must never be hardcoded in client-side code. Keys in JavaScript, APK/IPA binaries, or version control are extractable via: (1) Source code inspection (git history, public repos). (2) APK decompilation or IPA dumping. (3) Memory inspection (if keys are loaded at runtime). (4) Cloud storage misconfiguration (AWS S3, GCS, Azure Blob Storage). (5) Dependency injection in build artifacts. Exposure enables: (1) API abuse (data theft, DDoS via quotas). (2) Impersonation of the application. (3) Reverse engineering of API endpoints. (4) Analytics or billing fraud. Secure practices: (1) Never embed API keys in client code. Instead, use backend proxy endpoints that authenticate users and call the API on their behalf. (2) Rotate keys frequently and revoke compromised ones. (3) Scan code repositories with tools like TruffleHog, Gitleaks, YARA. (4) Use environment variables or secure credential management (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) for backend keys only. (5) Implement IP whitelisting and rate limiting per API key. (6) Use short-lived tokens (OAuth2 access tokens) instead of long-lived keys for client applications. (7) Add key usage monitoring and anomaly detection.
evaluation_criteria: Must identify hardcoding vectors (source code, binaries, git history, cloud storage), explain API key abuse impact, prescribe backend proxy pattern and secure credential management instead of client-side keys

scenario: Session tokens lack randomness or are predictable, allowing attackers to enumerate and hijack valid sessions without access to the session store
prompt: A web application generates session tokens using weak randomness: time-based IDs, sequential counters, or predictable PRNG seeds. A user authenticates and receives session token: '20240607001' (timestamp-based). An attacker: (1) observes a few valid session tokens from the application. (2) identifies the pattern (e.g., incrementing numbers, time-based). (3) generates valid session tokens by guessing or brute-forcing. (4) submits the guessed token in a cookie and is authenticated as a different user. (5) does not need to break into the session store; the token itself is the secret. Example: time-based token + loose validation = attacker predicts tokens for concurrent sessions. Explain token entropy requirements, prediction attacks, and cryptographic randomness.
reasoning_focus: Session token entropy, predictable token generation, session enumeration attacks
expected_answer: Session tokens serve as cryptographic proofs of authentication. Tokens must have sufficient entropy to prevent enumeration or prediction. Weak entropy sources (timestamp, sequential IDs, unseeded PRNG, or weak PRNG algorithms) enable brute-force or pattern-based attacks. An attacker observing a few tokens can predict future tokens and hijack sessions without server-side compromise. Example: timestamps have ~86,400 possible values per day; an attacker can brute-force all sessions from a day. Weak PRNG (rand(), time() seeding) is predictable if the attacker knows the seed. Secure token generation requires: (1) Cryptographically secure PRNG (os.urandom, crypto.getRandomBytes, SecureRandom in Java). (2) Minimum 128 bits of entropy (~22 base64 characters) for unpredictable tokens. (3) Constant-time comparison when validating tokens (prevent timing attacks). (4) Token invalidation on logout and timeout enforcement. (5) Binding tokens to IP or User-Agent to limit session hijacking impact. (6) Use libraries that generate tokens correctly (e.g., express-session, passport with configured session store). (7) Audit token generation in security reviews by checking RNG sources and entropy calculations.
evaluation_criteria: Must describe predictable token patterns and enumeration attacks, explain entropy requirements and weak PRNG vulnerabilities, prescribe cryptographically secure RNG and minimum token length (128 bits)

scenario: Refresh tokens lack rotation on use, allowing indefinite token replay if a refresh token is compromised or leaked
prompt: An OAuth2 provider issues long-lived refresh tokens (valid for 30 days) that can be reused across multiple token exchanges. A user obtains a refresh token: 'refresh_abc123xyz...'. An attacker: (1) intercepts the refresh token (via XSS, log disclosure, or compromised device backup). (2) stores the token for later use. (3) months later, even after the legitimate user has logged out and revoked sessions, uses the stored refresh token to request a new access token. (4) the authorization server accepts the request because the refresh token is still within its 30-day validity and no rotation mechanism was triggered. (5) attacker impersonates the user indefinitely. The legitimate user has no way to revoke the stolen token since the provider doesn't invalidate old refresh tokens upon each use. Explain refresh token replay risks, rotation mechanisms, and revocation strategies.
reasoning_focus: Refresh token replay and reuse, token rotation, revocation and invalidation
expected_answer: Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens without re-authentication. If refresh tokens are not rotated (issued a new token on each use and old token invalidated), a compromised token enables indefinite impersonation. Risks: (1) Replay attacks—attacker uses the token months later. (2) No revocation—legitimate user cannot immediately block a stolen token. (3) Session tying—attacker gains persistent access to all user resources. Token rotation mitigates these: (1) Sender-Constrained Tokens (DPOP, DPoP proof) bind tokens to the client's key pair, preventing reuse by attackers. (2) Refresh Token Rotation (RTR)—on each token exchange, issue a new refresh token and invalidate the old one. (3) Refresh Token Reuse Detection—if a refresh token is used twice, revoke all tokens issued from that chain and force re-authentication. (4) Refresh Token Expiry—set short lifetimes (7–30 days) and require periodic re-authentication. (5) Refresh Token Rotation on Logout—revoke all refresh tokens for the user. Implementation: (1) Store refresh token with a 'used' flag or generation number. (2) On exchange, check if token was already used; if so, revoke entire token family. (3) Log refresh token exchanges for anomaly detection. (4) Monitor for high-frequency exchanges indicating compromise.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain refresh token replay and indefinite impersonation mechanics, prescribe refresh token rotation with reuse detection and automatic family revocation, recommend monitoring for anomalous exchange patterns

scenario: HTTP Basic Authentication credentials transmitted in Base64 over unencrypted HTTP, exposing usernames and passwords to network sniffing
prompt: A legacy REST API uses HTTP Basic Authentication for client authentication. Clients send: 'Authorization: Basic dXNlcm5hbWU6cGFzc3dvcmQ=' (Base64 of 'username:password') over HTTP. An attacker: (1) performs packet sniffing on the network (WiFi, ISP, proxy). (2) captures HTTP requests containing the Authorization header. (3) decodes Base64 to extract plaintext credentials: username:password. (4) uses credentials to authenticate to the API and impersonate the client. (5) no HTTPS means credentials are visible to anyone on the network path. The API does not enforce HTTPS or detect multiple failed authentication attempts. Explain why Base64 is not encryption, HTTP transmission risks, and secure HTTP Basic Authentication practices.
reasoning_focus: HTTP Basic Authentication encoding vs. encryption, transport layer security, credential exposure
expected_answer: HTTP Basic Authentication sends credentials as Base64-encoded 'username:password' in the Authorization header. Base64 is encoding, not encryption—it's reversible without a key and provides no secrecy. Sending Basic Auth over HTTP is equivalent to sending plaintext credentials over the network. Any attacker with network visibility (ISP, WiFi, proxy, on-path gateway) can capture and decode credentials. Risks: (1) Credential theft and unauthorized access. (2) Impersonation of legitimate clients. (3) Lateral movement to other systems using the same credentials. (4) Compliance violations (HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GDPR). Secure practices: (1) Enforce HTTPS/TLS for all Basic Auth transmission; never use HTTP. (2) Use TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphers (TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384). (3) Implement certificate pinning in client libraries to prevent MITM. (4) Use token-based authentication (OAuth2, JWT) instead of Basic Auth when possible. (5) Rotate credentials regularly. (6) Log and monitor authentication attempts for anomalies and multiple failures. (7) Implement rate limiting on failed attempts. (8) Use client certificates (mTLS) for machine-to-machine authentication instead of shared secrets. For backward compatibility with existing APIs: mandate HTTPS, implement API key rotation, and migrate clients to modern auth.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain Base64 as encoding not encryption and HTTP transmission risks, prescribe mandatory HTTPS/TLS with certificate pinning, recommend migration to token-based or mTLS authentication

scenario: HMAC signatures use a weak or hardcoded secret key, enabling signature forgery and unauthorized API access
prompt: An API uses HMAC-SHA256 to sign requests. Each request includes a signature header: 'X-Signature: HMAC-SHA256(secret, method+path+body)'. The secret key is: (1) hardcoded in client libraries and version control, (2) a weak value like 'secret123' or the API key itself, (3) reused across all clients with the same value. An attacker: (1) obtains the secret via code inspection, repository access, or by observing API patterns. (2) crafts a forged request with a valid HMAC signature using the compromised secret. (3) the API validates the signature and accepts the forged request. (4) attacker can read, modify, or delete data without authentication. Weak secrets also enable brute-force attacks: attacker tries common secrets ('password', 'admin', 'secret') and succeeds. Explain HMAC security assumptions, secret key strength requirements, and signature bypass risks.
reasoning_focus: HMAC secret key entropy, signature forgery, weak cryptographic constants
expected_answer: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) proves message authenticity and integrity using a shared secret. Security depends entirely on secret entropy and secrecy. A weak secret (< 128 bits, predictable, or hardcoded) enables: (1) Brute-force attacks—attacker tries common values or dictionary attacks on the HMAC output. (2) Source code disclosure—if secret is in repositories, binaries, or logs, anyone with code access can forge signatures. (3) Signature reuse—attacker observes valid signatures and replays them. Risks: (1) Unauthorized data access. (2) API abuse (quota exhaustion, DoS). (3) Data tampering. (4) No accountability (attacker impersonates legitimate client). Secure HMAC usage: (1) Use cryptographically secure secret generation (os.urandom, minimum 256 bits of entropy). (2) Never hardcode secrets in code. Store in secure vaults (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault). (3) Use per-client secrets, not shared secrets. (4) Implement secret rotation (30–90 days). (5) Sign entire request (method, path, headers, body) to prevent tampering. (6) Include a timestamp and nonce to prevent replay attacks. (7) Implement rate limiting to slow brute-force attacks. (8) Monitor for repeated signature validation failures indicating compromise. (9) Consider rotating compromised secrets immediately. (10) For server-to-server auth, use mTLS or JWT-based approaches instead of shared HMAC secrets.
evaluation_criteria: Must identify weak secret patterns and brute-force/forgery vectors, explain HMAC security dependency on secret entropy, prescribe secure key generation, storage in vaults, per-client secrets, and timestamp/nonce inclusion

scenario: OIDC state parameter is not validated or enforced, allowing cross-site request forgery (CSRF) and authorization code interception
prompt: An OpenID Connect (OIDC) implementation fails to validate the 'state' parameter. The flow: (1) User clicks 'Login with Google' on app.example.com. (2) App redirects to Google authorization endpoint without including a state parameter or with a static/reused state value. (3) A CSRF attacker crafts a malicious link: 'https://app.example.com/login?code=attacker_authorization_code' and tricks the user into visiting it. (4) App accepts the authorization code without validating that it matches the original request. (5) Attacker's authorization code for attacker@gmail.com is exchanged for an access token. (6) User is logged in as the attacker, or the attacker gains access to the user's session. Alternatively, the authorization server returns a state parameter but the client ignores it. Explain CSRF in OIDC flows and state parameter validation requirements.
reasoning_focus: OIDC state parameter validation, CSRF in OAuth2/OIDC flows, authorization code binding
expected_answer: The OIDC authorization code flow is vulnerable to CSRF if the 'state' parameter is not used or validated. State is a random, unguessable value generated by the client, included in the authorization request, and returned by the authorization server in the redirect. The client must verify that the returned state matches the original. Omitting or reusing state enables: (1) CSRF attacks—attacker redirects user to authorization endpoint with attacker's credentials, obtaining an authorization code issued to the attacker but redeemable by the victim's browser. (2) Authorization code interception and reuse—attacker obtains an authorization code (via open redirect, history theft) and exchanges it for a token. (3) Session fixation—attacker fixes the victim's session to the attacker's account. Secure practices: (1) Generate state as cryptographically secure random value (minimum 128 bits) per authentication request. (2) Store state in a secure, session-bound store (HttpOnly session cookie, localStorage for SPAs with CSRF protection). (3) Verify that returned state exactly matches the stored state before proceeding. (4) Reject authorization responses with missing, invalid, or duplicate state values. (5) Use short-lived authorization codes (< 10 minutes) and one-time use enforcement (revoke on token exchange). (6) Bind authorization codes to client_id and redirect_uri. (7) Implement nonce parameter for implicit/hybrid flows. (8) Log and alert on state mismatch attempts.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain CSRF and authorization code interception vectors without state validation, prescribe cryptographically secure per-request state generation and strict validation, recommend one-time authorization code enforcement

scenario: mTLS certificate validation is disabled or incomplete, allowing attackers to present self-signed or invalid certificates and bypass mutual authentication
prompt: A service-to-service API uses mutual TLS (mTLS) with client certificate authentication. However: (1) the server does not validate the client certificate's CN (Common Name) or SAN (Subject Alternative Name) against the expected service identity. (2) self-signed certificates are accepted without verification against a trusted CA. (3) certificate chain validation is skipped due to misconfiguration (InsecureSkipVerify in Go, VERIFY_NONE in OpenSSL). (4) certificate expiration is not checked. (5) certificate revocation (CRL, OCSP) is not enforced. An attacker: (1) generates a self-signed certificate with an arbitrary CN. (2) submits it to the mTLS server. (3) server accepts it as valid due to disabled validation. (4) attacker is authenticated as a service and gains unauthorized API access. This is particularly dangerous when combined with DNS spoofing or ARP poisoning. Explain mTLS validation requirements and certificate pinning strategies.
reasoning_focus: mTLS certificate validation, certificate chain verification, certificate pinning, revocation checking
expected_answer: Mutual TLS (mTLS) authenticates both client and server using certificates. Security requires rigorous validation of the client certificate: (1) Verify certificate signature against a trusted CA (not self-signed unless explicitly pinned). (2) Validate certificate chain to root CA. (3) Check certificate expiration dates and not-before times. (4) Verify CN or SAN (Subject Alternative Name) matches the expected service identity. (5) Enforce certificate revocation via CRL or OCSP to prevent use of compromised certificates. (6) Optionally, use certificate pinning to bind to specific certificates. Disabled validation (InsecureSkipVerify, VERIFY_NONE) is a critical misconfiguration that defeats the purpose of mTLS. An attacker can present any certificate, even self-signed, and be authenticated. Risks: (1) Unauthorized service-to-service access. (2) No accountability (attacker impersonates a service). (3) Lateral movement within a service mesh. Secure practices: (1) Enable full certificate chain validation in all clients and servers. (2) Use a private CA for service certificates; enforce trust only in that CA. (3) Validate CN/SAN against a whitelist of expected identities. (4) Check expiration and revocation status on every connection (or cache with TTL). (5) Implement certificate rotation (30–90 days). (6) Use certificate pinning for critical connections—store hash of expected certificate and reject others. (7) Log and alert on certificate validation failures. (8) Use service mesh tooling (Istio, Linkerd) to automate mTLS and certificate management. (9) Monitor for certificate theft or compromise.
evaluation_criteria: Must identify disabled/incomplete validation vectors (self-signed acceptance, skipped chain validation, missing CN/SAN checks), prescribe strict certificate chain validation with revocation checking, recommend certificate pinning and service mesh automation

scenario: Personal Access Tokens (PATs) for API access lack scope limitations or expiration, enabling overprivileged and long-lived token abuse
prompt: A developer platform (GitHub-like) allows users to create Personal Access Tokens (PATs) for API access. A user creates a PAT with: (1) no explicit scopes or all scopes enabled (read, write, delete, admin). (2) no expiration date (valid forever). (3) displayed once but stored in plaintext in logs or development tools. An attacker: (1) obtains the PAT (via leaked repository, developer machine compromise, or logs). (2) uses the PAT to access all API endpoints (repos, secrets, users, billing). (3) the PAT grants admin privileges indefinitely. (4) attacker deletes repositories, steals secrets, or creates backdoor accounts. (5) legitimate user is unaware until significant damage occurs. Even if the user rotates the token, old PATs are sometimes cached in Docker config files, CI/CD tools, or shell history. Explain PAT security risks, scope limitations, and secure PAT management practices.
reasoning_focus: PAT overprivilege and expiration, token scope enforcement, PAT rotation and invalidation
expected_answer: Personal Access Tokens (PATs) are long-lived credentials granting programmatic access to APIs. Overprivileged PATs enable: (1) Unauthorized access to all resources (repos, secrets, settings, billing). (2) Indefinite impersonation if expiration is not enforced. (3) Privilege escalation if admin scopes are enabled by default. (4) Lateral movement if the token is shared across tools. Risks: (1) Token theft via log disclosure, insecure storage, or dependency compromise. (2) Insider threats (disgruntled developers abusing PATs). (3) Supply chain attacks (compromised CI/CD tool using a PAT). (4) Compliance violations (unrotated, overprivileged tokens). Secure PAT practices: (1) Create PATs with minimal required scopes; use scope limitations (e.g., 'repo:read' instead of 'repo:read+write+admin'). (2) Set explicit expiration dates (30–90 days); force rotation before expiry. (3) Do not display PAT after creation; regenerate if leaked or suspected compromised. (4) Audit PAT usage (source IP, endpoints accessed, timestamps). (5) Implement PAT revocation for unused tokens (e.g., > 30 days without use). (6) Store PATs only in secure credential managers (1Password, Vault, GitHub secrets), not in code, config files, or environment. (7) Scan repositories and CI/CD configs for hardcoded tokens (TruffleHog, Gitleaks). (8) Monitor for anomalous PAT activity (bulk deletions, rapid requests, access from unexpected IPs). (9) Rotate PATs immediately upon compromise suspicion. (10) For service accounts, prefer short-lived tokens (JWT with 15-minute expiry) instead of static PATs.
evaluation_criteria: Must identify overprivilege vectors (all scopes enabled, no expiration, shared tokens) and abuse patterns, prescribe minimal scope limitation and short-lived expiration with forced rotation, recommend secure storage in credential managers and anomaly monitoring

scenario: JWT validation library accepts tokens with 'alg: none', allowing unsigned tokens to be treated as valid.
prompt: A Node.js API uses a JWT library to verify incoming authentication tokens. The library is configured to accept tokens without strict algorithm validation. An attacker crafts a JWT with 'alg': 'none' in the header, sets their desired 'sub' claim to an admin user ID, and omits the signature entirely. If the server doesn't explicitly reject tokens with 'alg: none', the library treats the token as valid. Explain how the alg:none vulnerability bypasses JWT signature verification, describe the attacker's steps to exploit it, and prescribe the fix.
reasoning_focus: JWT algorithm confusion attack allowing unsigned token acceptance
expected_answer: JWT tokens contain three parts: header, payload, signature. The header specifies the algorithm used for signing (HMAC, RSA, etc.). The 'alg: none' value indicates the token is unsigned and requires no signature verification. A vulnerable JWT library may accept this as a valid algorithm choice. An attacker encodes a JWT manually with header {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}, payload {"sub":"admin","iat":1234567890}, and no signature portion (the token ends with a dot). When the server validates this token, it checks the algorithm from the header, finds 'none', and skips signature verification entirely. This completely bypasses authentication. The attacker can then impersonate any user, including administrators, by controlling the 'sub' claim. Prevention requires: (1) never accepting 'alg: none' tokens—explicitly reject them, (2) whitelist allowed algorithms (e.g., HS256, RS256 only), (3) verify the algorithm matches your signing method, and (4) use a well-maintained JWT library with secure defaults.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain why 'alg: none' bypasses signature verification; must describe the attacker's token construction and claim manipulation; must prescribe algorithm whitelisting and explicit rejection of 'none'

scenario: OAuth2 authorization server doesn't require PKCE for public clients, allowing authorization code interception attacks.
prompt: A mobile application uses OAuth2 authorization code flow to authenticate users against a third-party identity provider. The application is classified as a 'public client' (no client secret). The OAuth2 server doesn't enforce Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE), which means the application doesn't include a code_challenge parameter in the authorization request. An attacker intercepts the authorization code returned to the redirect URI (via network sniffing or compromised network) and exchanges it directly for an access token without needing the code_verifier. Since PKCE wasn't used, the attacker doesn't need to know any secret to complete the exchange. Explain the authorization code interception attack, why PKCE prevents it, and the implementation requirements.
reasoning_focus: OAuth2 PKCE absence allows authorization code replay without proof of origin
expected_answer: PKCE (RFC 7636) is a security extension for OAuth2 public clients that prevents authorization code interception. In a standard authorization code flow, the client requests an authorization code, which is sent back through the user's browser to a redirect URI. If an attacker intercepts this code (via network sniffing, compromised DNS, or XSS), they can send it to the token endpoint and receive an access token if no additional proof of origin is required. PKCE mitigates this by requiring the client to create a random code_verifier (43-128 characters) and send its SHA256 hash (code_challenge) in the initial authorization request. When exchanging the code for a token, the client must provide the original code_verifier. The server verifies that SHA256(code_verifier) matches the code_challenge from the authorization request. Even if an attacker intercepts the authorization code, they cannot complete the token exchange without the code_verifier, which the attacker never sees. Implementation: (1) public OAuth2 clients MUST use PKCE, (2) servers must require code_challenge in authorization requests for public clients, (3) servers must validate code_verifier against code_challenge before issuing tokens, and (4) use S256 (SHA256) method, not 'plain'.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain how authorization code interception leads to token theft; must describe PKCE's code_verifier/code_challenge mechanism; must prescribe server-side PKCE enforcement for public clients

scenario: Session tokens are generated using weak pseudo-random number generation or predictable patterns (e.g., sequential IDs, current timestamp).
prompt: A Python web application generates session tokens by seeding Python's random module with the current Unix timestamp and then generating a token. Another application uses session tokens that are simply the Base64 encoding of an incrementing counter. An attacker observes a few valid session tokens and, due to the weak randomness or predictable pattern, calculates the next expected token. The attacker can then forge tokens or hijack other users' sessions. Describe how weak token generation enables session hijacking, explain why cryptographically secure randomness is essential, and prescribe proper token generation.
reasoning_focus: Weak RNG in session token generation enables predictability and forgery
expected_answer: Session tokens serve as proof of authentication and must be cryptographically unpredictable. Weak token generation occurs when: (1) using Python's random module (seeded from predictable sources like time), (2) using sequential or increment-based patterns, (3) using timestamps or user IDs as token components, or (4) using insufficient entropy (too short tokens). An attacker who observes a few tokens can identify the pattern and predict the next valid token. For example, if tokens are Counter_123, Counter_124, Counter_125, the attacker simply guesses Counter_126. Similarly, if Python's random is seeded with time, an attacker knowing the approximate token creation time can brute-force the seed and regenerate all subsequent tokens. A compromised session token grants full impersonation of the user until expiration or logout. Prevention: (1) use cryptographically secure RNGs (os.urandom in Python, SecureRandom in Java, crypto.getRandomBytes in Node.js), (2) generate at least 128 bits of entropy (256 bits preferred), (3) use established libraries like uuid4, (4) never include user IDs or predictable values in tokens, and (5) set appropriate TTLs and enforce rotation.
evaluation_criteria: Must identify weak RNG sources and predictable patterns; must explain how pattern recognition enables token forgery; must prescribe cryptographically secure RNG and minimum entropy

scenario: HMAC signatures use weak or short secrets that can be brute-forced or are hardcoded in code.
prompt: A REST API authenticates requests by including an HMAC-SHA256 signature in the Authorization header. The signature is computed over the request method, path, and body using a 'secret' shared between the client and server. An attacker discovers that the secret is only 4 characters long (e.g., 'test') and hardcoded in a client library published on GitHub. The attacker brute-forces the secret using a simple dictionary or learns it from the public source code. Once the secret is known, the attacker can forge valid signatures for any request, impersonating any authenticated client. Explain HMAC vulnerability from weak secrets, describe the attack, and prescribe secure secret management.
reasoning_focus: HMAC authentication fails when secrets are weak, short, or exposed
expected_answer: HMAC (Hash-Based Message Authentication Code) uses a shared secret and hash function to produce a message authentication code. The security of HMAC depends entirely on the secrecy and strength of the shared secret. If the secret is weak (short, predictable, or common), an attacker can brute-force it. A 4-character secret has only 2^32 possible values; even with SHA256, this is easily brute-forceable in minutes. Hardcoding secrets in source code (especially public repositories) exposes them permanently. Once an attacker knows the secret, they can forge valid HMAC signatures for any message, completely bypassing authentication. Additionally, if the same secret is shared across all clients (a common mistake), one compromised client leaks the secret for all traffic. Prevention: (1) use cryptographically random secrets of at least 128 bits (32 characters Base64), (2) never hardcode secrets in source code—use environment variables or key management systems, (3) use unique secrets per client/API key rather than a shared global secret, (4) rotate secrets regularly, (5) store secrets securely in vaults (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault), and (6) use HMAC only for authentication with APIs you control; for untrusted parties, use asymmetric signatures (RSA, ECDSA).
evaluation_criteria: Must explain HMAC's dependence on secret strength and secrecy; must describe brute-force attack and hardcoding exposure; must prescribe strong random secrets, environment management, and per-client separation

scenario: HTTP Basic Authentication credentials (username:password Base64-encoded) are transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, allowing network-level credential interception.
prompt: A legacy API server supports HTTP Basic Authentication over plain HTTP (not HTTPS). Credentials are encoded as Base64 in the 'Authorization: Basic <base64(username:password)>' header. An attacker on the same network (or intercepting traffic via ARP spoofing, DNS hijacking, or compromised ISP) captures HTTP traffic. Base64 encoding is trivially reversible (it's just encoding, not encryption). The attacker decodes the Authorization header and obtains plaintext username and password. The attacker then uses these credentials to access the API with the user's full privileges. Explain why HTTP + BasicAuth is insecure, describe the credential recovery process, and prescribe secure authentication transport.
reasoning_focus: BasicAuth over HTTP exposes credentials via network interception and trivial Base64 decoding
expected_answer: HTTP Basic Authentication transmits credentials in the Authorization header as Base64-encoded 'username:password'. Base64 is encoding, not encryption—any actor with network visibility can extract the header and decode it to plaintext in seconds. HTTP (unencrypted) sends all traffic in plaintext, visible to network intermediaries, ISPs, on shared networks, and anyone with ARP spoofing or DNS hijacking capabilities. An attacker can passively sniff traffic or actively intercept it via MITM and immediately obtain valid credentials. Once obtained, credentials provide full authenticated access. Additionally, BasicAuth is stateless—credentials are resent with every request, expanding the window of exposure. Prevention: (1) NEVER use BasicAuth over HTTP—always require HTTPS/TLS, which encrypts the entire request including the Authorization header, (2) HTTPS provides confidentiality and server authentication, preventing credential interception and MITM attacks, (3) consider replacing BasicAuth with token-based schemes (Bearer tokens, OAuth2) for better security properties, (4) enforce HTTPS with HSTS headers, (5) regularly rotate credentials, and (6) monitor for credential leaks.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain Base64 encoding is not encryption; must describe network interception risks (ARP spoofing, passive sniffing); must prescribe HTTPS requirement and credential rotation

scenario: Refresh tokens are not rotated upon reuse, allowing indefinite unauthorized access if an old refresh token is compromised.
prompt: An OAuth2 provider issues access tokens (15-minute TTL) and refresh tokens (30-day TTL) to mobile and web clients. When a client's access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to the token endpoint to obtain a new access token. The provider validates the refresh token but does NOT invalidate it or issue a new refresh token in response (refresh token reuse is allowed). If an attacker steals a user's refresh token (via compromised device, network interception, or app vulnerability), the attacker can use that same token indefinitely (for 30 days until the token naturally expires) to repeatedly obtain new access tokens without needing the user's password. The legitimate user has no way to revoke the stolen token short of changing their password. Explain refresh token theft risk, why token rotation mitigates it, and implement refresh token rotation.
reasoning_focus: Non-rotating refresh tokens enable indefinite impersonation after theft
expected_answer: Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens when the short-lived access token expires. If a refresh token is compromised, the attacker can repeatedly use it to generate valid access tokens indefinitely (until the refresh token expires naturally). Unlike a stolen access token (which expires in minutes), a stolen refresh token provides persistent unauthorized access. Additionally, if the same refresh token is reused across multiple token-endpoint calls, the attacker's usage is indistinguishable from legitimate usage if the user logs in from another device. Refresh Token Rotation mitigates this by issuing a new refresh token with each token-endpoint call and invalidating the old one. If an attacker uses a stolen refresh token, the server detects that an old (already-rotated-out) refresh token is being reused and rejects the request. Legitimate clients always receive fresh tokens and only the latest refresh token is valid. To detect stolen tokens, the server should also flag 'unexpected' parallel refresh token usage (e.g., the same user obtaining tokens from two different clients/devices simultaneously). Implementation: (1) issue a new refresh token with each token endpoint call, (2) invalidate the old refresh token immediately, (3) persist valid refresh tokens in a database or cache, (4) detect and reject reuse of retired refresh tokens, (5) implement device/client binding to detect anomalous refresh patterns, and (6) add short reuse detection windows (if two different clients use the same token within seconds, flag breach).
evaluation_criteria: Must explain persistent access risk from non-rotating refresh tokens; must describe rotation mechanism and old-token invalidation; must prescribe reuse detection and parallel-usage monitoring

scenario: OAuth2 authorization flow doesn't validate or properly use the 'state' parameter, enabling CSRF attacks on the OAuth flow itself.
prompt: A web application implements OAuth2 login via a third-party provider (e.g., Google). During the authorization flow, the user is redirected to the OAuth provider with a 'state' parameter meant to prevent CSRF. However, the application doesn't validate the state parameter upon redirect back, or it uses a static/hardcoded state value instead of a unique per-request value. An attacker crafts a malicious authorization URL pointing to their own redirect_uri and tricks a victim into clicking it. The victim is redirected to the OAuth provider, which asks for permission, and then the attacker's application receives an authorization code (which they can then exchange for a token). Alternatively, if state validation is missing, an attacker can pre-generate an authorization code and redirect the victim to a URL that logs them into a malicious account the attacker controls. Explain the state parameter's purpose, describe the CSRF attack scenario, and prescribe proper state validation.
reasoning_focus: Missing or weak state parameter validation enables CSRF and authorization code hijacking in OAuth2 flows
expected_answer: The 'state' parameter in OAuth2 is a CSRF protection mechanism. When the application initiates an OAuth flow, it generates a unique random state value, stores it in the user's session (or a cryptographically signed cookie), and includes it in the authorization request URL. When the OAuth provider redirects the user back to the application with an authorization code, the authorization code is paired with the same state value. The application verifies that the returned state matches the stored session state, confirming that the redirect came from the same user's session and not from an attacker's forged request. If state validation is missing or state is reused, an attacker can trick a user into authorizing OAuth access (e.g., by visiting a crafted URL), and the application will accept the authorization code without verifying that the user initiated the request. This can lead to account takeover (if the user is logged in via OAuth) or cross-session authorization attacks. Additionally, weak state generation (e.g., sequential values, predictable patterns) allows attackers to forge valid state values. Implementation: (1) generate cryptographically random state values per authorization request (at least 128 bits), (2) store state in the session with a short TTL (5-15 minutes), (3) on redirect callback, verify that the returned state exactly matches the stored session state, (4) reject requests with missing, mismatched, or expired state values, (5) use PKCE in addition to state for public clients, and (6) implement SameSite cookies to provide additional CSRF defense.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain state parameter's CSRF defense purpose; must describe authorization code hijacking and account takeover scenarios; must prescribe random state generation, session storage, and strict validation

scenario: OpenID Connect implementations verify JWT signature but skip audience ('aud') claim validation, allowing ID tokens from one application to be accepted by another.
prompt: An organization runs multiple OIDC clients (web applications) that authenticate users via a centralized OIDC provider. The OIDC provider issues ID tokens that include the 'aud' (audience) claim identifying which client the token was issued for. Each application verifies the ID token's signature using the provider's public key but doesn't validate the 'aud' claim. An attacker obtains an ID token intended for Application A (e.g., via XSS or log exposure). The attacker then submits this token to Application B's /callback endpoint. Application B verifies the token signature (which is valid, since it was issued by the trusted provider) and extracts the user ID from the 'sub' claim, logging the user in as the original user from Application A. The attacker has now impersonated a user from a different application. Explain the role of the 'aud' claim, describe the cross-application token substitution attack, and prescribe proper OIDC validation.
reasoning_focus: OIDC audience validation prevents tokens from being misused across multiple relying parties
expected_answer: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is built on JWT. The ID token contains claims like 'sub' (subject/user ID), 'aud' (audience/intended client), 'iss' (issuer), and 'exp' (expiration). The 'aud' claim specifies which client(s) the token was issued for and should only be accepted by that client. Signature verification ensures the token hasn't been tampered with, but it doesn't verify the token was meant for the current application. If Application B only checks the signature and doesn't validate 'aud', a token issued for Application A can be reused at Application B. Since the OIDC provider issued the token with a valid signature, the cryptographic check passes, and the application trusts the 'sub' claim (user ID). The attacker gains unauthorized access to another user's account in Application B. This is especially dangerous in shared OIDC setups where multiple applications trust the same provider. Prevention: (1) every OIDC client MUST validate the 'aud' claim matches its own client_id, (2) validation must occur before trusting the 'sub' claim or any user-derived claims, (3) reject tokens with mismatched or missing 'aud', (4) also validate 'iss' (issuer) to ensure the token came from the expected provider, (5) validate 'exp' (expiration), (6) validate 'iat' (issued at) is not in the future, and (7) use a well-maintained OIDC library that enforces these validations by default.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain the purpose of the 'aud' (audience) claim in OIDC; must describe the cross-application token substitution and impersonation attack; must prescribe mandatory 'aud' validation before trusting user claims

scenario: SAML assertion signatures are verified but signature validation logic contains a bypass (e.g., accepting assertions without signatures, XML signature wrapping, or weak digest algorithms).
prompt: An enterprise uses SAML 2.0 for single sign-on (SSO). A service provider (SP) receives SAML assertions from an identity provider (IdP) and verifies the XML signature. However, the signature validation logic has a critical flaw: it accepts SAML assertions where the signature verification fails if the assertion contains any comment nodes or if the Signature element is missing but the assertion has previously been seen. Alternatively, the SP uses a deprecated digest algorithm (MD5) that is collision-susceptible. An attacker modifies a captured SAML assertion by: (1) removing the Signature element, (2) adding XML comments, or (3) changing claims (e.g., setting NameID to an admin user) while keeping the outer structure valid. The SP's signature validation fails to detect the tampering and accepts the modified assertion. Alternatively, the attacker generates a collision against the MD5 digest and replaces the signed assertion with a malicious one that hashes to the same value. Explain SAML signature bypass attacks, describe the implications, and prescribe secure SAML validation.
reasoning_focus: SAML assertion tampering via signature validation flaws enables authentication forgery
expected_answer: SAML 2.0 uses XML signatures to authenticate and verify the integrity of assertions. A SAML assertion contains user claims (NameID, attributes, authentication context) and is wrapped in an XML Signature element that cryptographically signs the assertion content. The service provider verifies the signature using the IdP's public certificate. However, SAML signature validation is complex due to XML's flexibility: (1) incomplete validation (e.g., accepting unsigned assertions or missing Signature elements), (2) XML signature wrapping attacks where an attacker embeds a valid signed assertion inside another structure and modifies the outer claims, (3) comment-based bypasses where XML comments are excluded from signature validation, allowing claims after comments to be modified, (4) weak digest algorithms (MD5, SHA-1) vulnerable to collision or pre-image attacks, allowing attackers to forge assertions with identical digests. An attacker who successfully tampers with a SAML assertion can change the NameID (user identity) to an admin account, add group memberships, or extend session duration. Prevention: (1) use a modern SAML library that canonicalizes XML before validation (to prevent wrapping/comment attacks), (2) mandate XML Signature presence—reject unsigned assertions, (3) verify the signature is applied to the correct element (not wrapped or nested), (4) use only SHA-256 or stronger digest algorithms, (5) validate the IdP certificate and its expiration, (6) check assertion timestamps (NotBefore, NotOnOrAfter), (7) verify the Recipient attribute matches the SP URL, (8) validate the Issuer matches the expected IdP, and (9) use a library that follows the OASIS SAML 2.0 standard strictly.
evaluation_criteria: Must describe SAML assertion components and signature role; must identify at least two signature bypass techniques (XML wrapping, weak digests, comment injection); must prescribe XML canonicalization, algorithm strength, and recipient validation

scenario: Personal Access Tokens (PATs) have predictable structures or insufficient entropy, allowing enumeration or forgery attacks.
prompt: A DevOps platform issues Personal Access Tokens (PATs) to users for API authentication. The PAT format is 'pat_' followed by a 12-character alphanumeric string. An attacker observes a few valid PATs (e.g., pat_aB1cD2eF3gH4, pat_aB1cD2eF3gH5) and notices the tokens are sequential or follow a simple pattern. The attacker writes a script to enumerate possible PATs by iterating through the 12-character space and checking validity by attempting API calls (e.g., listing repositories or API usage). Valid PATs return successful responses; invalid ones return 401. Due to the small keyspace and no rate limiting, the attacker successfully enumerates valid PATs. Alternatively, if the PAT generation uses weak randomness (e.g., seeded from timestamp), an attacker can predict tokens issued around the same time. Describe PAT enumeration and generation attacks, explain the required token properties, and prescribe secure PAT handling.
reasoning_focus: Weak PAT generation and lack of rate limiting enable enumeration and forgery attacks on API keys
expected_answer: Personal Access Tokens (PATs) are long-lived API keys used for programmatic API access. PAT security depends on: (1) high entropy generation (sufficient randomness to make enumeration infeasible), (2) sufficient length (at least 32 characters), and (3) rate limiting on failed token validation to prevent brute-force enumeration. If PATs are short (12 characters) or use only alphanumeric characters, the keyspace is reduced, making brute-force feasible. If generation uses weak RNG seeded by time, an attacker can predict tokens. If the API has no rate limiting on authentication failures, an attacker can enumerate valid tokens by making repeated requests and observing successful responses vs. 401 errors. Additionally, if PAT format is predictable (e.g., all start with 'pat_' and follow a known pattern), attack surface grows. An attacker who enumerates valid PATs gains full API access as that user, including reading data, modifying configurations, or deleting resources. Prevention: (1) PATs must be generated using cryptographically secure RNG with at least 256 bits of entropy (43+ Base64 characters), (2) use a long, random prefix to increase entropy and make pattern recognition difficult, (3) implement rate limiting on token validation endpoints (e.g., max 5 failures per minute per IP), (4) implement bot detection (CAPTCHA) after repeated failures, (5) hash PATs in the database using bcrypt or Argon2, not plaintext or weak hashes, (6) add token scopes to limit API permissions, (7) enable token expiration (encourage short-lived tokens; long-lived PATs are high-risk), (8) log and monitor unusual token usage patterns, and (9) provide users with token rotation and revocation mechanisms.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain PAT enumeration via predictable format or weak RNG; must describe rate-limiting lack and brute-force feasibility; must prescribe cryptographic RNG, sufficient entropy/length, rate limiting, and hashing

scenario: A JWT library or implementation permits the 'alg=none' algorithm in the JWT header, allowing unsigned tokens or tokens with no signature verification.
prompt: An API endpoint accepts JWT tokens with various algorithms (HS256, RS256, alg=none). The token validation logic does not explicitly reject 'alg=none' and treats such tokens as valid if they parse correctly as JSON. An attacker crafts a JWT with alg=none, sets arbitrary claims (e.g., sub=admin, role=superuser), and the server accepts it as valid because the library defaults to skipping signature verification for unsigned tokens. Walk through how an attacker constructs an unsigned JWT, explain why 'alg=none' is dangerous, and describe the validation logic that prevents this attack.
reasoning_focus: JWT algorithm validation, unsigned token acceptance, signature bypass
expected_answer: The 'alg=none' algorithm in JWT specifications allows tokens without cryptographic signatures. Many JWT libraries, by default, accept unsigned tokens if the algorithm field is explicitly set to 'none'. An attacker exploits this by constructing a token with an arbitrary payload and alg=none, bypassing all signature verification. The header.payload.signature format still holds, but the signature portion is empty. If the validation logic does not explicitly reject 'alg=none' and does not enforce a whitelist of acceptable algorithms (e.g., only RS256 or HS256), unsigned tokens are accepted. The attack is trivial to execute: use any JWT encoder to set alg=none, craft any payload, and submit. Mitigation requires: (1) explicitly disallowing 'alg=none' in token validation, (2) enforcing a strict whitelist of allowed algorithms per context, (3) using a robust JWT library that rejects unsigned tokens by default, and (4) configuring the library to fail on algorithm mismatch.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain alg=none bypass mechanics and token construction; must identify why libraries default to accepting unsigned tokens; must prescribe explicit algorithm whitelist enforcement

scenario: JWT header includes a 'kid' (Key ID) field that is used to select the signing key from a key store without proper validation, allowing an attacker to inject an arbitrary kid value to force use of an attacker-controlled key.
prompt: An API uses the JWT 'kid' header parameter to look up the correct public key for signature verification. The kid is stored in a key store (e.g., a JWKS endpoint or local config). An attacker intercepts or observes a valid JWT and learns the key storage mechanism. The attacker then crafts a new JWT with a forged kid value that points to a key the attacker controls (e.g., a kid='attacker-key' that maps to a public key the attacker published on an accessible server or injects into the key store via a misconfigured endpoint). The server looks up 'attacker-key' in the key store, finds the attacker's public key, and validates the JWT against it, treating the forged token as valid. Explain the kid injection attack, the key lookup mechanism, and how to prevent it.
reasoning_focus: JWT kid injection, key lookup validation, attacker-controlled key insertion
expected_answer: The JWT 'kid' (Key ID) header field identifies which key should be used to verify the signature. In implementations that use a key store or JWKS endpoint, the kid is used as a lookup key. If the server does not validate or whitelist which kid values are acceptable, an attacker can inject a kid pointing to a key the attacker controls. For example, if the key store allows public submission of keys or if the kid resolves to an attacker-controlled endpoint, the attacker's key is used for verification. The attack flow: (1) craft a JWT payload with desired claims, (2) sign it with an attacker-controlled private key, (3) set kid in the header to point to the attacker's public key, (4) the server looks up kid, retrieves the attacker's public key, and validates the signature. Mitigation: (1) maintain a strict whitelist of allowed kid values and keys, (2) prevent external input from directly selecting keys (validate kid against a hardcoded list), (3) use immutable key stores or signed JWKS endpoints, (4) implement key pinning to bind kids to specific key IDs, and (5) reject unknown kid values outright.
evaluation_criteria: Must describe kid injection mechanics and key lookup exploitation; must explain how attacker-controlled keys enter the key store; must prescribe kid whitelist validation and key immutability

scenario: OAuth2 implicit flow (response_type=token) returns access tokens directly in the URL fragment without an authorization code exchange, exposing tokens to browser history, referrer headers, and interception.
prompt: An OAuth2 provider offers the implicit flow for SPAs and mobile apps. A client application redirects to the authorization endpoint with response_type=token, requesting direct token delivery. The authorization server returns the access token in the URL fragment: /callback#access_token=xyz&token_type=Bearer. An attacker can capture the token via: (1) browser history if the user visits a compromised site after login, (2) the Referer header if the user clicks a link from the authenticated page, (3) network packet sniffing if HTTPS is misconfigured, or (4) XSS in the SPA that exfiltrates the token from the fragment. The attacker then uses the stolen token to impersonate the user. Explain the implicit flow token exposure risk, why the authorization code flow is safer, and alternatives for SPAs.
reasoning_focus: OAuth2 implicit flow token exposure, browser history/Referer risks, SPA token handling
expected_answer: The OAuth2 implicit flow (response_type=token) returns access tokens directly in the URL fragment as an optimization to reduce round-trips. However, this exposes tokens to multiple attack vectors: (1) Browser history: tokens in the fragment persist in browser history and are accessible to any malicious script, (2) Referer headers: if the authenticated page links to an external site, the browser sends the Referer header containing the entire URL with the token, (3) Server logs: while fragments are not logged server-side, intermediate proxies or APIs may log full URLs, (4) XSS vulnerabilities: JavaScript can read window.location.hash and exfiltrate tokens. The authorization code flow mitigates this by: (1) returning an authorization code (short-lived, single-use, opaque) in the fragment, (2) exchanging the code for tokens in a backend-to-backend call with client secret validation. For SPAs, the recommended approach is: (1) use the authorization code flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange), (2) validate the code server-side and return tokens via secure, HttpOnly cookies, (3) never expose raw access tokens to JavaScript.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain implicit flow token exposure vectors including browser history and Referer leaks; must contrast with authorization code flow security; must prescribe code flow with PKCE for SPAs

scenario: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is implemented but the server does not properly validate the code_challenge or accepts authorization requests without a code_challenge, allowing code interception and reuse.
prompt: An OAuth2 provider supports PKCE but the authorization server does not enforce it for public clients (or treats it as optional). A public client initiates a standard authorization flow without PKCE parameters (no code_challenge). An attacker intercepts the authorization code during the redirect (via network sniffing, malware, or XSS in the redirect URL). Since PKCE is not enforced, the attacker can exchange the intercepted code for an access token without knowing the code_verifier—the server does not validate it. Alternatively, the server accepts a PKCE challenge but does not properly validate the code_verifier hash (e.g., accepts any verifier if a challenge was present, or does not compute the hash correctly). Walk through the interception attack, explain why PKCE is necessary for public clients, and describe proper PKCE validation.
reasoning_focus: PKCE validation bypass, authorization code interception, public client token theft
expected_answer: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) protects public clients (browser apps, mobile apps) from authorization code interception. The flow: (1) client generates a random code_verifier, (2) derives a code_challenge from the verifier using SHA256, (3) sends code_challenge to the authorization server, (4) receives an authorization code, (5) exchanges the code with the code_verifier. The server validates that SHA256(code_verifier) == code_challenge. If PKCE is not enforced or validation is skipped, an attacker who intercepts the authorization code can exchange it for a token without the verifier. PKCE bypass occurs when: (1) the server does not require code_challenge for public clients, (2) the server does not validate code_verifier, (3) the server accepts any code_verifier if code_challenge is present, or (4) the hash validation is incorrect. Mitigation: (1) mandate PKCE for all public clients and authorization requests without client secrets, (2) verify that code_verifier when provided matches SHA256(code_challenge) or plain code_challenge (depending on method), (3) store code_challenge with the authorization code and invalidate it after one use, (4) use constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks, and (5) log and alert on PKCE validation failures.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain PKCE flow and code_verifier validation mechanics; must describe code interception and reuse when PKCE is bypassed; must prescribe validation enforcement and hash verification

scenario: API keys or authentication credentials are hardcoded in source code, committed to version control, exposed in logs, error messages, or publicly accessible configuration files.
prompt: A microservice retrieves API keys from environment variables at startup, but during development, a developer hardcodes a production API key in a config file (e.g., config.js, .env.example) for convenience and commits it to the repository. The key is also logged during authentication failures: 'Authentication failed with key: sk_live_abc123xyz'. A user monitoring production logs or reviewing the codebase discovers the key. The attacker can now: (1) directly call the API using the exposed key without authentication, (2) exhaust rate limits and cause denial of service, (3) access sensitive data if the key grants read/write permissions, or (4) pivot to other services if the key is reused. Explain how hardcoded keys are discovered, why they are dangerous, and how to prevent exposure.
reasoning_focus: Hardcoded API key discovery, credential exposure in version control and logs, privilege escalation via key reuse
expected_answer: API keys are symmetric credentials that grant access to protected resources. When hardcoded in source code or configuration files, they are discoverable through: (1) repository scanning (git log, GitHub search), (2) decompiled binaries or bundled client code, (3) production logs or error messages that echo keys, (4) environment leaks in stack traces, (5) misconfigured public repositories. Once discovered, the key provides direct API access without further authentication. The attacker can impersonate the service, read/write data, and if the key is shared across services, compromise additional systems. Mitigation: (1) never commit secrets to version control—use .gitignore and pre-commit hooks to block secret patterns, (2) inject credentials via environment variables or secret management systems (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), (3) rotate keys regularly and invalidate old keys, (4) never log authentication credentials; instead log token hashes or IDs, (5) use separate keys with minimal scopes for each service/environment, (6) implement key expiration and approval workflows, and (7) scan repositories and dependencies with tools like git-secrets, TruffleHog, or Snyk.
evaluation_criteria: Must identify discovery vectors including version control scanning and log leakage; must explain privilege escalation and cross-service compromise from key reuse; must prescribe secret management and key rotation practices

scenario: Session IDs are not regenerated after successful authentication, allowing an attacker to pre-set a session ID and trick a victim into authenticating with that ID, then use the known ID to hijack the session.
prompt: A web application creates a session ID when a user first visits (pre-authentication). The application does not regenerate the session ID after login. An attacker sets a victim's session ID via URL parameter manipulation, XSS, or cookie injection (e.g., via a malicious link: /login?sessionId=attacker_known_value or Set-Cookie injection). The victim visits the malicious link, logs in normally with their credentials, but the application reuses the attacker-supplied session ID. After login, the attacker can use the known session ID to access the victim's authenticated session without credentials. The attacker gains full account access. Explain session fixation mechanics, the attack chain, and proper session token regeneration.
reasoning_focus: Session fixation attack mechanics, pre-set session ID reuse, lack of token regeneration after login
expected_answer: Session fixation occurs when an application fails to regenerate the session ID after authentication. The attack flow: (1) attacker generates or predicts a session ID, (2) tricks the victim into using this ID (via malicious link, XSS injecting a Set-Cookie, or URL parameter), (3) victim authenticates with the application while unknowingly using the attacker-supplied session ID, (4) the application does not invalidate or regenerate the ID upon login and associates the session ID with the victim's account, (5) attacker uses the known session ID to access the authenticated session. Session fixation is possible because: (1) session IDs are not regenerated after login, (2) session creation is not tied to the authentication event, (3) the application accepts externally supplied session IDs. Mitigation: (1) always regenerate the session ID upon successful authentication—invalidate the old pre-auth session ID and issue a new one, (2) use the same session ID regeneration mechanism for privilege escalation (e.g., when a user role changes), (3) ensure session IDs are cryptographically random and unpredictable, (4) implement secure cookie flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), (5) validate session origin and user agent on each request to detect anomalies, and (6) implement session timeout and re-authentication prompts for sensitive operations.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain the pre-set session ID injection and reuse mechanics; must describe why lack of regeneration enables fixation; must prescribe post-login session ID regeneration and token invalidation

scenario: SAML assertion XML signature is vulnerable to wrapping or comment injection attacks, allowing an attacker to inject or modify claims (e.g., user ID, role) while the signature remains valid over the original content.
prompt: A SAML identity provider issues a signed SAML assertion: <Assertion><Subject><NameID>user@example.com</NameID></Subject><AuthnStatement>...</AuthnStatement></Assertion>. The signature covers the Assertion element. A service provider verifies the signature but does not strictly validate the XML structure. An attacker obtains the assertion and injects a comment or additional element before the signature: <Assertion><!-- malicious comment with role=admin --><Subject><NameID>attacker@evil.com</NameID></Subject>...</Assertion>. Alternatively, the attacker wraps the signature in a different XML structure or duplicates the Assertion element, moving the signature to a parent that contains the modified claims. The service provider parses the XML and processes the injected claims, while the signature validator operates on a different part of the tree, causing a validation bypass. The attacker gains elevated privileges. Explain XML signature wrapping, canonicalization issues, and proper SAML validation.
reasoning_focus: SAML XML signature wrapping, canonicalization attacks, XML parsing ambiguities
expected_answer: SAML assertions are XML documents signed with asymmetric keys. Signature wrapping attacks exploit ambiguities in XML parsing and canonicalization. The attack: (1) attacker obtains a signed SAML assertion, (2) injects additional XML elements (comments, child elements, duplicates) that modify the claimed identity or attributes, (3) the signature reference points to a specific element (e.g., the original Subject), but the XML parser may process injected sibling or parent elements, (4) the signature verifier confirms the signature is valid over the referenced element (which remains unchanged), (5) the service provider processes the injected claims from the newly parsed XML, effectively bypassing authorization. Root causes: (1) XML parsers may handle comments and duplicates differently, (2) signature canonicalization (C14N) may not cover the entire assertion as parsed, (3) service providers may not enforce strict schema validation, (4) signature scope ambiguity—signature covers only a subset of the assertion. Mitigation: (1) use strict XML schema validation (enforce single Assertion per response), (2) verify signature digest covers all claimed attributes, not just the Subject, (3) apply strict canonicalization (exclusive C14N 1.0 or 1.1) and ensure the service provider parses using the same canonicalization, (4) reject assertions with comments, multiple Assertions, or unexpected nesting, (5) use SAML 2.0 best practices (encrypted assertions, signed metadata), and (6) test with known SAML attack payloads.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain XML injection and signature wrapping mechanics; must identify canonicalization and parsing ambiguity root causes; must prescribe strict schema validation and signature scope enforcement

scenario: BasicAuth credentials (username:password) are base64-encoded and transmitted in the Authorization header, but the encoding is mistaken for encryption, leading to unencrypted transmission over unencrypted channels or insufficient protection.
prompt: A REST API uses HTTP BasicAuth for client authentication. The server and client base64-encode the credentials (username:password) and transmit them in the Authorization header: Authorization: Basic dXNlcm5hbWU6cGFzc3dvcmQ=. A developer assumes base64 encoding provides encryption and deploys the API over HTTP (not HTTPS). An attacker performs network sniffing and intercepts the HTTP request. The attacker base64-decodes the header and recovers the plaintext credentials: username:password. The attacker now has the client's credentials and can authenticate as that client, gaining unauthorized API access. The developer mistakenly believed base64 encoding was a security mechanism. Explain why BasicAuth encoding is not encryption, the risks of unencrypted BasicAuth, and proper BasicAuth deployment.
reasoning_focus: Base64 encoding vs. encryption, BasicAuth plaintext transmission, credential exposure over unencrypted channels
expected_answer: BasicAuth uses base64 encoding for formatting, not encryption. Base64 is a reversible encoding scheme: anyone can decode Base64(username:password) to recover the plaintext credentials in seconds. The misconception arises because encoding and encryption are visually similar (both render text unreadable), but they serve different purposes: encoding is for transport/serialization, encryption is for confidentiality. An attacker who intercepts HTTP traffic can base64-decode the Authorization header and extract credentials. HTTP BasicAuth is safe only when transmitted over HTTPS (TLS/SSL encryption), which encrypts the entire HTTP request and response, rendering the base64-encoded credentials meaningless to a network eavesdropper. Mitigation: (1) always use HTTPS (TLS 1.2 or later) for BasicAuth, (2) prefer OAuth2 bearer tokens over BasicAuth for API authentication, (3) do not rely on encoding for security—use cryptographic encryption, (4) implement rate limiting on failed authentication attempts to mitigate brute-force attacks, (5) consider certificate pinning for high-value clients, (6) avoid logging full Authorization headers—log token hashes only, and (7) rotate credentials periodically.
evaluation_criteria: Must clarify the distinction between base64 encoding and encryption; must explain credential exposure over HTTP and recovery via base64 decoding; must prescribe HTTPS enforcement and token-based alternatives

scenario: OpenID Connect ID tokens (intended for user identification) are misused as access tokens for API authorization, or ID tokens are accepted without proper validation (signature, nonce, aud claims).
prompt: An application uses OpenID Connect to authenticate users. The OIDC provider returns an ID token (containing user info and signed by the provider) and an access token (for API calls). The application mistakenly uses the ID token as the access token when calling APIs (e.g., Authorization: Bearer <id_token>). An attacker obtains a victim's ID token (via XSS, network sniffing, or token leakage) and uses it to call protected APIs that expect only access tokens. Alternatively, the application accepts an ID token without verifying the signature, nonce, or 'aud' (audience) claim. An attacker crafts a forged ID token with arbitrary claims (e.g., sub=admin_user_id) and if the application blindly trusts the claims, the attacker is granted admin access. Explain the distinction between ID and access tokens, why mixing them is dangerous, and proper token validation.
reasoning_focus: OIDC ID token vs. access token roles, ID token misuse for authorization, missing signature/nonce/aud validation
expected_answer: OpenID Connect defines two token types: (1) ID tokens: signed JWTs containing user identity claims (sub, email, name), intended for authentication and user identification, (2) Access tokens: opaque or JWT tokens intended for API authorization and resource access. ID tokens are not meant for API calls—they are user identifiers, not authorization credentials. The attack: (1) attacker obtains an ID token, (2) submits it to an API expecting an access token, (3) the API extracts claims from the ID token and treats them as authorization grants, allowing API access. ID tokens lack API-specific metadata (scopes, resource indicators) and use shorter TTLs. Using ID tokens for APIs is dangerous because: (1) ID tokens are user-bound, not application-bound—any holder of the ID token can impersonate the user, (2) ID tokens may lack audience restrictions (aud claim) specific to the API, (3) scope validation is missing. Proper validation requires: (1) verify ID token signature using the provider's public key (JWKS endpoint), (2) validate aud claim matches the application's client ID, (3) validate nonce (if used in the authorization flow) to prevent replay attacks, (4) check token expiration (exp claim), (5) use access tokens (not ID tokens) for API calls, (6) validate access token scope and audience for each API resource, and (7) implement refresh token rotation.
evaluation_criteria: Must distinguish ID token and access token purposes and roles; must explain ID token misuse for API authorization and forged token acceptance; must prescribe signature, nonce, aud, and scope validation

scenario: OAuth2 scope validation is weak or missing, allowing an attacker to request or claim elevated scopes (e.g., admin, write permissions) beyond what the user authorized, or to modify scope claims in the access token.
prompt: An OAuth2 authorization server issues access tokens with scopes (e.g., read:profile, write:data, admin:users). A user initiates a login and is prompted to grant scopes—the application requests 'read:profile' and the user approves. However, the authorization server or token endpoint does not validate that the granted scopes match the requested scopes, or the validation is weak. An attacker intercepts the authorization code or refresh token and exchanges it while requesting additional scopes: /token?code=xyz&scope=read:profile%20write:data%20admin:users. The server does not validate against the original authorization grant and issues a token with all requested scopes. Alternatively, if tokens are JWTs, the attacker crafts a token with elevated scopes. The attacker can now access protected resources and perform actions beyond the user's authorization. Explain scope escalation mechanics, proper scope validation, and scope-based access control implementation.
reasoning_focus: OAuth2 scope validation bypass, scope claim forgery, missing scope enforcement on resource servers
expected_answer: OAuth2 scopes define the permissions granted to an access token. Scope validation must occur at multiple points: (1) authorization server: validate that scopes requested in the authorization request match approved scopes (presented to the user for consent), (2) token endpoint: validate that scopes requested during code/refresh token exchange do not exceed the original grant, (3) resource server: validate that the access token's scopes permit the requested operation. Scope escalation occurs when: (1) the authorization server does not enforce scope boundaries—accepting any requested scope without user consent, (2) the token endpoint allows scope inflation—issuing a token with scopes not approved by the user, (3) resource servers do not check token scopes—accepting any token regardless of scope. Mitigation: (1) at authorization time, store the approved scopes with the authorization code, (2) during token exchange, validate that requested scopes do not exceed stored approved scopes—reject or filter to the approved subset, (3) on resource servers, always validate the access token's scope against the requested operation (e.g., write:data required for POST, read:profile required for GET /profile), (4) use signed access tokens (JWTs) to prevent claim modification and store scope list as a claim verified by resource servers, (5) implement scope mapping—map internal permission models to OAuth2 scopes, and (6) log scope mismatches and escalation attempts.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain scope escalation through weak server-side validation and scope claim forgery; must identify validation points across authorization server, token endpoint, and resource server; must prescribe scope boundary enforcement and resource-level validation

scenario: JWT token validation does not enforce algorithm type, allowing attacker to craft unsigned tokens (alg=none).
prompt: A web application validates JWT tokens by checking the signature. The validation library can be misconfigured to accept the 'none' algorithm. An attacker crafts a JWT with alg='none' and no signature, setting arbitrary claims (user_id, role=admin). The application's JWT verification function receives the token and, due to improper algorithm checking, accepts it as valid. The attacker is now authenticated as admin. Explain why alg=none is dangerous, which JWT libraries are vulnerable to misconfiguration, and how to enforce a whitelist of algorithms.
reasoning_focus: Algorithm enforcement in JWT validation and signature verification bypass via alg=none
expected_answer: The 'alg' header field specifies the cryptographic algorithm used to sign the JWT. Setting alg='none' indicates the token is unsigned. Vulnerable JWT libraries (especially older versions or Python's PyJWT before 2.0) may accept alg='none' if the developer doesn't explicitly whitelist allowed algorithms. To exploit this: (1) decode an existing JWT to see header and payload structure; (2) modify claims (user_id, role); (3) set alg='none' and remove the signature; (4) submit the crafted token. The application accepts it because it skips signature verification for 'none' tokens. Prevention: explicitly whitelist algorithms (HS256, RS256, ES256 as applicable), reject 'none' by default, and ensure verification always performs signature validation. Use libraries with algorithm enforcement enabled by default.
evaluation_criteria: Must explain why alg=none bypasses signature checks, identify vulnerable JWT libraries and versions, and prescribe algorithm whitelisting with validation rejection of 'none' algorithm

scenario: JWT 'kid' (key ID) header is not validated; attacker injects a custom kid pointing to attacker-controlled key.
prompt: A JWT provider issues tokens with a 'kid' header identifying which key was used to sign the token. The provider maintains a JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) endpoint listing public keys. A client application does not validate that the 'kid' in the JWT header is an expected, legitimate kid from the JWKS. An attacker signs a JWT with their own key, sets the 'kid' to a custom value (e.g., 'attacker-key'), and sends it to the application. The application retrieves the JWKS, attempts to find the kid, and when it doesn't exist, it either rejects the token or (in poorly designed systems) falls back to an insecure default. Explain the kid injection attack, why validation is critical, and how to safely handle unknown kids.
reasoning_focus: JWT 'kid' header validation and key ID injection attacks
expected_answer: The 'kid' (key ID) header identifies which signing key was used, enabling key rotation and multi-key scenarios. An attacker can inject a custom 'kid' value to bypass key validation. Attack scenarios: (1) if the JWKS endpoint is user-controlled or unsanitized, the attacker can host a JWKS with their public key and the app fetches it; (2) if the app falls back to a symmetric key (shared secret) when the kid is unknown, the attacker can request the shared secret or brute-force it; (3) if the app doesn't validate the kid strictly, it may use an unexpected key. Prevention: (1) validate that the 'kid' exists in your authorized JWKS before verifying the signature; (2) use only public keys from a trusted JWKS endpoint under your control; (3) implement kid caching with integrity verification; (4) reject tokens with unknown kids immediately. Never fall back to defaults or accept user-supplied JWKS URLs.
evaluation_criteria: Must describe kid injection attack vectors, explain why kid validation prevents key substitution, and prescribe whitelist-based kid validation against trusted JWKS

scenario: JWT signed with HS256 using a weak, short secret (e.g., 'password123'), allowing brute-force signature forgery.
prompt: A JWT service signs tokens using HMAC-SHA256 with a shared secret of 'secret123' (8 characters). An attacker intercepts a valid JWT token and knows it's signed with a weak symmetric key (common in poorly configured systems). The attacker runs a brute-force tool (e.g., jwt-cracker, hashcat) against common passwords and wordlists. Within minutes, the attacker discovers the secret 'secret123'. Now possessing the secret, the attacker can forge arbitrary JWTs, impersonating any user. Explain entropy requirements for HMAC secrets, detection of weak secrets, and the risk if a secret is compromised.
reasoning_focus: HMAC secret entropy and JWT forgery via weak shared secret compromise
expected_answer: HMAC-based JWT signing relies on a shared secret's entropy. Weak secrets (short, dictionary words, predictable patterns) are vulnerable to brute-force attacks. A 32-byte (256-bit) random secret is minimum; 64 bytes is recommended. Attack: capture a JWT, feed it to a brute-force tool with wordlists, and recover the secret within hours or minutes depending on entropy.
